summary:
SPHEREx Time Explorer is a web application that lets anyone watch a selected region of the sky change over time, like a short video, using NASA SPHEREx images. Users enter sky coordinates and a field of view. The application queries the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive, retrieves only the required cutouts, aligns them, and plays them back so that moving objects such as comets, asteroids, nearby stars and brown dwarfs stand out.

To make motion easier to spot, the application supports median subtraction, frame differences, frame stacking and proper-motion tracking. Users can click on a point to see its spectrum across all 102 SPHEREx infrared bands. It also features a Gaia DR3 star overlay, shareable URLs, an embeddable mode and a Turkish/English interface. Everything runs directly in the browser, and a new data release only requires a small configuration change.

SPHEREx produces far more images than any one person can analyze. By making image comparison fast and accessible, the application helps volunteers and professionals discover moving objects, much as citizen science has done with earlier surveys. Live on: https://spherexdata.com.tr
details:
What it does

SPHEREx Time Explorer is a tool that makes it easier to see how the sky changes over time. Users simply enter a set of sky coordinates (in degrees or hh mm ss), select an area between 1 and 60 arcminutes, and the tool creates a short video using NASA's SPHEREx observations of that region.

Objects such as comets, asteroids, nearby stars, and brown dwarfs appear as moving dots, making it much easier to spot changes between observations.

How it works

When a user enters coordinates, the tool first checks NASA/IPAC's Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) to find observations covering that part of the sky. Rather than downloading entire images, it only retrieves the smaller sections needed for the selected area.

We built a lightweight FITS reader that runs directly in the browser. It processes each image, uses its World Coordinate System (WCS) information to align observations on the same north-up grid, and resamples them so they can be compared accurately.

Once the images are aligned, users can explore them in several ways. They can view the original frames, subtract the median image to highlight changes, compare individual frames, or stack multiple observations together.

For objects with significant proper motion, such as WISE 0855 or Barnard's Star, users can enter their motion values to keep them centered throughout the sequence.

There are a few other useful features as well. Clicking on a point reveals its brightness across all 102 SPHEREx bands, with known absorption wavelengths of water and other ices marked for reference. A Gaia DR3 overlay, provided through VizieR, helps identify known stars. This makes it easier to notice moving objects that don't match any cataloged star.

Users can also share their current view through a URL, embed the tool on other websites, export individual frames as PNG files, or open the same region in Aladin.

Why it matters

SPHEREx is expected to produce an enormous amount of imaging data, far more than any single research team could realistically examine on its own.

Volunteers have already helped identify numerous comets, brown dwarfs, and nearby stars by comparing astronomical images. We wanted to build on that idea by creating a tool that makes this process faster and more accessible.

The goal was to make something free, easy to use, and available to everyone, whether they're students, astronomy enthusiasts, volunteers, or researchers. There's nothing to install, and because the project is a static website, it can be hosted on almost any web server. Updating the tool for a new data release is also straightforward and only requires changing one line in the settings file.

What we used

The project was built using plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with canvas for rendering the images. We deliberately avoided frameworks and complicated build processes to keep things simple.

A small PHP script handles requests to IRSA, while a Python script runs the website locally during development and testing. The finished site is hosted on shared hosting.

For astronomical data and visualization, we use NASA/IPAC IRSA for SPHEREx spectral images, Gaia DR3 through VizieR, and Aladin for exploring sky regions.

We also created a small rotating 3D wireframe model of the SPHEREx spacecraft as part of the interface.

Claude, an AI assistant, was used throughout development to help with coding, documentation, and some of the presentation text.

What makes it different

Most astronomical image viewers are designed to display one image at a time. SPHEREx Time Explorer takes a different approach by treating each sky location as a sequence of observations rather than a single picture.

By bringing techniques such as median subtraction, frame comparison, and image stacking directly into the browser, the tool makes moving objects easier to spot without requiring specialized software or a complicated setup.

Limitations and future plans

We've tested the tool using both a local mock server and real SPHEREx observations, including a sequence containing 200 frames.

There are still a few limitations. IRSA occasionally returns temporary errors, so we added automatic retries to the request relay. We also included a Simulation mode, allowing users to explore the interface even when there's no internet connection.

At the moment, the tool doesn't account for image distortion terms or bad-pixel flags. It also uses a single center wavelength for each image, which means the spectral information is still approximate.

One of our main goals for the next version is to improve spectral accuracy by reading wavelength information for individual pixels and making better use of the available image quality flags.
